definition:
Idolatry is giving to anything created the trust, love, service, and worship that belong to God alone. In its plainest form it is bowing down to a carved or cast image; in Scripture it also includes worshiping the true God through an image he has forbidden, serving the gods of the nations alongside him, and, as the New Testament makes explicit, setting the heart on money, appetite, or anything else in God's place. Behind every form lies an exchange: the glory of the living God traded for something made. The prophets add a warning that runs through the whole Bible: people become like what they worship. Idols that cannot see or hear produce worshipers who cannot see or hear God. This study traces how Scripture exposes idolatry from Genesis to Revelation. The study of God treats the one living God whom idolatry replaces, and the study of sin treats the wider turning from God of which idolatry is the root form.

Hebrew has a rich and often scornful vocabulary for idols. Pesel is a ‘carved image’, the word in the second commandment (Exodus 20:4), and massekah a ‘cast’ or molten image (Exodus 32:4). 'Elilim, ‘worthless things’ or ‘nothings’, sounds like 'elohim, ‘God’ or ‘gods’, and Psalm 96:5 plays on the two: “all the gods of the nations are idols” (literally, ‘all the 'elohim of the peoples are 'elilim’). Hevel, ‘vapor’ or ‘breath’, is used of idols as empty things (Deuteronomy 32:21; Jeremiah 2:5). Gillulim, used about forty-eight times and thirty-nine of them in Ezekiel, is a contemptuous term whose origin is debated; some scholars connect it with a word for dung. Shiqquts, ‘detestable thing’, names foreign gods such as Milcom (1 Kings 11:5), and teraphim are household images (Genesis 31:19; 1 Samuel 15:23). Tselem, ‘image’, is used both for idols (2 Kings 11:18) and for humanity made in God's image (Genesis 1:27). In Greek, eidōlon means ‘image’ and then ‘idol’, eidōlolatria is ‘idolatry’, eidōlothuton is ‘food sacrificed to idols’ (Acts 15:29), and Luke's word for Athens, kateidōlos (Acts 17:16), means a city ‘full of idols’.
ot:
Genesis sets the scene before any idol appears. God makes humanity “in His own image” (Genesis 1:27), so the one image of God the world is meant to contain is the living human being who represents God's rule. Idolatry reverses that order: people who were made to image God make images of gods. The patriarchs come out of an idolatrous world. Joshua recalls that Abraham's father Terah and his family “lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods” (Joshua 24:2). Rachel steals her father's household idols (Genesis 31:19), and before Jacob returns to Bethel he tells his household, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you” and buries them under the oak at Shechem (Genesis 35:2, 4).

At Sinai the first two commandments ground the prohibition of idols in rescue: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before Me. You shall not make for yourself an idol” (Exodus 20:2-4). The reason given is that the LORD is “a jealous God” (Exodus 20:5), and he even bears the name Jealous (Exodus 34:14). The word qanna' describes the exclusive claim of a husband on his wife, not petty envy, and the prophets will develop that marriage picture. Deuteronomy explains the ban on images from Israel's own experience: “you saw no form of any kind on the day the LORD spoke to you out of the fire at Horeb” (Deuteronomy 4:15). God revealed himself by his word, not by a shape. The golden calf shows that idolatry can happen while the true God is being named. The people want “gods who will go before us,” Aaron makes a calf, and they say, “These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt,” but Aaron proclaims “a feast to the LORD” (Exodus 32:1, 4-5). They were trying to worship the LORD through an image they could see and manage. A later psalm names the result: “They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox” (Psalm 106:20). Moses' closing song adds that behind the idols stand real spiritual powers, since Israel “sacrificed to demons, not to God” (Deuteronomy 32:17).

The history of Israel in the land is largely a history of idolatry and its consequences. Judges runs in cycles that begin, “the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals” (Judges 2:11), and it shows private idolatry mixing with the worship of the LORD in Micah's household shrine (Judges 17:5). When the Philistines put the captured ark in Dagon's temple, Dagon is found “fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD” (1 Samuel 5:3). Samuel tells Saul that “arrogance is like the wickedness of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15:23), where the Hebrew word is teraphim, household idols: self-will is itself a form of idol worship. Solomon in old age follows Ashtoreth and Milcom (1 Kings 11:5). Jeroboam, founding the northern kingdom about 930 BC, sets up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan and repeats Aaron's words, “Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28). Many scholars think the calves were meant as pedestals for the invisible LORD rather than as other gods, which makes the story a sharper warning. Elijah on Mount Carmel confronts a people who want both the LORD and Baal: “How long will you waver between two opinions?” (1 Kings 18:21). The historian explains the fall of Samaria in 722 BC by the northern kingdom's idolatry (2 Kings 17:7-18). Hezekiah even breaks up the bronze serpent Moses had made, because Israel had been burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4): a God-given object can become an idol. Idolatry is tied to injustice and bloodshed, above all the sacrifice of children to Molech, which Josiah ends by defiling Topheth (2 Kings 23:10; Psalm 106:37-38).

The prophets expose idolatry with grief and scorn. Hosea describes it as adultery against the LORD (Hosea 4:12) and says of the calf of Samaria, “a craftsman made it, and it is not God” (Hosea 8:6). Isaiah's great satire describes a man who cuts down a tree, burns half to bake his bread, and makes a god of the rest, saying, “Save me, for you are my god” (Isaiah 44:17), without asking, “Shall I bow down to a block of wood?” (Isaiah 44:19). The idols of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, must be carried on weary animals (Isaiah 46:1), while the LORD says to Israel, “I have made you, and I will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4). Jeremiah calls idols “scarecrows in a cucumber patch” (Jeremiah 10:5) and gives the sharpest diagnosis: Israel “followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves” (Jeremiah 2:5), in Hebrew ‘went after vapor and became vapor’. His people have forsaken “the fountain of living water” to dig “broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13). The Psalms state the principle: idols have mouths but cannot speak, and “Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8; 135:18). Ezekiel sees the elders worshiping images in the dark (Ezekiel 8:12) and hears that they “have set up idols in their hearts” (Ezekiel 14:3). The problem is inward before it is outward, and so is the cure: God promises, “I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols. I will give you a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:25-26). In Babylon, Daniel's three friends refuse to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue (Daniel 3:18). After the exile the Jewish community became fiercely opposed to images, and the desecration of the temple by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV in 167 BC, which Daniel 11:31 calls “the abomination of desolation” in the reading of Jewish and Christian interpreters from the Maccabean period on, provoked the Maccabean revolt.
nt:
The New Testament assumes the Old Testament's verdict on images and presses the question inward. Jesus is tempted to gain the kingdoms of the world if he will “fall down and worship” the devil, and he answers with Deuteronomy: “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (Matthew 4:9-10). He names money as the rival master that competes for the same loyalty God claims: “No one can serve two masters,” and “You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24). Mammon, Aramaic for wealth, functions as a god when it is trusted and served. Yet Jesus himself receives worship: the disciples in the boat “worshiped Him, saying, ‘Truly You are the Son of God’” (Matthew 14:33), and Thomas confesses, “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). An angel refuses John's worship (Revelation 19:10) and Herod dies for accepting divine honors (Acts 12:22-23), but Jesus accepts it. The church confesses that this is not idolatry, because the Son is himself God, “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15; 2 Corinthians 4:4). In him God has given the one true image that the second commandment forbade Israel to make.

Acts shows the gospel meeting the idols of the Greco-Roman world. Stephen recalls the calf, “rejoicing in the works of their hands” (Acts 7:41). At Lystra, when the crowd tries to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas as gods, the apostles call them to “turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth” (Acts 14:15). The Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to “abstain from food sacrificed to idols” (Acts 15:29). In Athens Paul's spirit is provoked to see a city “full of idols” (Acts 17:16), and he tells the Areopagus that since human beings are God's offspring, “we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man's skill and imagination” (Acts 17:29). The living image of God is humanity, and the risen Man will judge the world (Acts 17:31). In Ephesus the silversmith Demetrius stirs a riot because Paul “says that man-made gods are no gods at all” (Acts 19:26), and the trade that depended on the goddess Artemis is threatened: idolatry and economics are bound together.

Paul gives the fullest analysis. In Romans 1 idolatry is the root of human sin: people who knew God “neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him” and “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles” (Romans 1:21, 23), echoing Psalm 106:20 and Jeremiah 2:11. They “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25), and God gave them over to the desires they had chosen. Conversion is described as turning “to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). In 1 Corinthians 8 Paul agrees that “an idol is nothing at all in the world” and restates Israel's confession of the one God so that it includes Jesus: “for us there is but one God, the Father,” and “there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:4, 6). Yet in chapter 10 he warns, “flee from idolatry” (1 Corinthians 10:14), because though the idol is nothing, “the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons” (1 Corinthians 10:20), and a person cannot share “the table of the Lord and the table of demons too” (1 Corinthians 10:21). Food bought in the market may be eaten freely, but not at the cost of a weaker believer's conscience (1 Corinthians 10:25-28). Paul also extends the category to desire: he lists idolatry among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20) and calls greed “idolatry” (Colossians 3:5; Ephesians 5:5). Of some he says “their god is their belly” (Philippians 3:19). Whatever commands a person's ultimate trust and devotion functions as a god.

John's first letter ends, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21), directly after confessing that Jesus Christ “is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). Revelation shows churches in Pergamum and Thyatira tempted to eat food sacrificed to idols as a way of fitting into civic and trade life (Revelation 2:14, 20). After the trumpet plagues the rest of humanity still worships “idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk” (Revelation 9:20), echoing Psalm 115. The beast from the earth commands people to make an image of the first beast and kills those who will not worship it (Revelation 13:14-15), which many interpreters connect with the worship of Roman emperors in the cities of Asia. The book ends with idolaters outside the holy city (Revelation 21:8; 22:15) and God's servants seeing his face (Revelation 22:4). The story that began with humanity made in God's image ends with that image restored in those who worship the Lamb.

keyTexts.why: Humanity is made in God's image. The world already contains God's chosen image, which is why making images of God or gods reverses the created order.
The first two commandments forbid other gods and images, grounded in the exodus and in God's jealous covenant love. Idolatry is a breach of relationship, not only of rule.
The golden calf is made while the people proclaim a feast to the LORD. Idolatry can be the attempt to worship the true God on terms people can see and control.
Israel saw no form at Horeb, only heard a voice, so it must make no image of God. God is known by his word, not by a shape.
Elijah confronts a people wavering between the LORD and Baal. The contest shows the silence of the idol and the living God who answers.
Idols have mouths, eyes, and ears that do nothing, and those who make and trust them become like them. The Bible's fullest statement that we become what we worship.
Isaiah's satire of the man who bakes bread with half a log and worships the other half. The idol is a lie the deceived heart cannot see through.
God's people exchanged their Glory for what does not profit, forsaking the fountain of living water for broken cisterns. Idolatry is both folly and betrayal.
Elders who have set up idols in their hearts come to consult the prophet. Idolatry begins inwardly, before any image is made.
Paul tells the Athenians that God is not like an image made by human skill, since people are God's offspring, and calls them to repent before the risen Judge.
Paul traces human sin to the exchange of God's glory for images and the worship of the creature rather than the Creator.
An idol is nothing, and there is one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ. Paul restates Israel's confession of the one God with Christ inside it.
Though idols are nothing, demons stand behind pagan sacrifice, and believers cannot share both the Lord's table and the table of demons.
Greed is idolatry. Paul extends the category from images to the desires that take God's place in the heart.
The letter confesses Jesus Christ as the true God and then ends by warning believers to keep themselves from idols.

history:
Judaism treated idolatry, avodah zarah (‘foreign worship’), as among the gravest of sins. A whole tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud bears that name and governs contact with idolatrous practice, and the Talmud lists idolatry with sexual immorality and murder as the three sins a Jew must die rather than commit (Sanhedrin 74a). Maimonides, in the Mishneh Torah (Laws of Idolatry 1:1), traced idolatry to an early error in which people honored the stars as God's servants and then came to worship them in his place. The early church inherited this conviction and paid for it. Christians refused to offer incense to the gods or to the emperor's image, and the Roman governor Pliny the Younger, writing to the emperor Trajan about 112, described testing accused Christians by asking them to do exactly that. Tertullian's On Idolatry (around 200) warned believers against trades and customs that involved them in pagan worship.

The great controversy over images came in the Byzantine church. Iconoclasm, the policy of destroying religious images, began under Emperor Leo III in the 720s and 730s. John of Damascus defended icons in his treatises on the divine images, arguing that since the invisible God had become visible in the incarnation, Christ could be depicted. The Second Council of Nicaea (787), the seventh ecumenical council, restored icons and distinguished latreia, the worship due to God alone, from the honorable veneration (proskynēsis) given to icons, which passes to the person they depict. A second period of iconoclasm (815 to 843) ended with the restoration of icons in 843, celebrated in the Eastern churches as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. In the West the Frankish court's Libri Carolini (around 790) objected to parts of the Greek settlement.

The Reformation reopened the question. Andreas Karlstadt called for the removal of images in 1522, Zurich removed images from its churches in 1524 under Huldrych Zwingli's leadership, and iconoclastic riots followed in parts of Switzerland, the Netherlands, and Scotland. Martin Luther opposed forced removal in his Invocavit sermons (1522) and allowed images for teaching and remembrance, while his Large Catechism (1529) defined a god as whatever a person's heart clings to and relies on, making the first commandment a matter of trust. John Calvin (Institutes 1.11-12) described the human mind as a continual factory of idols and rejected images of God in worship. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Questions 94 to 98) defines idolatry as trusting something in place of or alongside the true God and forbids images of God, and the Westminster Larger Catechism (1647, Question 109) forbids making any representation of God, of all or any of the three persons. The Council of Trent's decree on sacred images (1563) reaffirmed the veneration of images of Christ, Mary, and the saints, while insisting that no divinity is believed to be in them. The churches also number the commandments differently: Jewish tradition counts ‘I am the LORD your God’ as the first word; Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join the prohibitions of other gods and of images; and the Orthodox, Reformed, and Anglican churches, following an older division found in Philo, Josephus, and Origen, count the ban on images as a separate second commandment.

Missions raised the question in new forms. In China, Jesuits following Matteo Ricci judged Confucian rites for ancestors to be civil honors that converts could keep, while others judged them idolatrous; Pope Clement XI condemned the rites in 1715, and Pius XII relaxed the ban in 1939. Modern theologians have given more attention to idolatry as a matter of the heart and of culture. G. K. Beale's We Become What We Worship (2008) traced the principle of Psalm 115 through the canon, and Timothy Keller's Counterfeit Gods (2009) applied the biblical diagnosis to money, sex, and power.

differ.view: Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic: icons venerated, God alone worshiped
differ.body: Following the Second Council of Nicaea (787), these churches hold that the incarnation changed what may be depicted. The invisible God forbade Israel to make images of him, but in Christ God became visible, and so Christ, Mary, and the saints may be portrayed. Icons and images are honored, not worshiped; the veneration passes to the person represented, as honor shown to a portrait passes to the one it portrays. They point to the cherubim God commanded over the ark (Exodus 25:18-22) as proof that the second commandment never forbade all religious images, only the worship of made things. Rejecting icons, they argue, implicitly denies that the Son truly took visible flesh.

differ.view: Lutheran and many Anglican: images for teaching, not devotion
differ.body: Lutherans, following Luther's Invocavit sermons and his Large Catechism, locate idolatry chiefly in the heart's trust. Images such as the crucifix and biblical scenes may stay in churches as reminders and teaching aids, provided they are not worshiped or trusted, and forced destruction of images can itself become a new law. Many Anglicans hold a similar middle position. The first commandment is broken wherever the heart relies on anything but God, whether or not an image is involved, and the gospel frees Christians to use images without superstition.

differ.view: Reformed and Presbyterian: no images of God in worship
differ.body: The Reformed tradition, following Calvin, the Heidelberg Catechism, and the Westminster Standards, treats the ban on images as its own commandment governing how God is worshiped. God is to be worshiped only as he has commanded, and he gave Israel a word, not a form (Deuteronomy 4:15-16). Images of God, and for many in this tradition images of Christ as well, are therefore excluded from worship, since a picture cannot represent his deity and would draw devotion to a human invention. Christ's own image is the preached word and the sacraments he appointed. Reformed Christians differ among themselves about pictures of Jesus outside worship, such as in children's Bibles or films.

differ.view: Where the line falls in culture: conscience and custom
differ.body: A further debate concerns customs rather than images: ancestral rites, civic ceremonies, festival meals, and national symbols. Some Christians, following Paul's freedom to eat market meat (1 Corinthians 10:25-27) and the Jesuit accommodation in China, hold that customs can be received as civil honors once their religious meaning is removed or reinterpreted. Others, following Paul's warning that pagan sacrifice involves demons (1 Corinthians 10:20) and the refusal of early martyrs even to offer incense, hold that participation compromises witness and must be refused. Both sides appeal to 1 Corinthians 8 to 10, and both agree that conscience, love for weaker believers, and exclusive loyalty to Christ must guide the decision.

errors:
The church has rejected several misunderstandings. One treats idolatry as only an ancient problem of statues, so that a person without a carved image is free of it; Jesus' warning about money, Paul's calls to flee idolatry and his naming of greed as idolatry, and Ezekiel's idols of the heart all refuse that comfort. Another treats idols as mere nothings and so dismisses their power; Paul says both that the idol is nothing and that demons stand behind the sacrifice (1 Corinthians 8:4; 10:20), and Scripture shows idolatry enslaving whole societies in injustice and bloodshed. The church has also rejected the opposite claim, that the worship of Christ is idolatry: the Son is not a creature but true God, and the councils of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) confess him so. To refuse him worship is to refuse God.

A subtler distortion is the idolatry of good things. Nehushtan was made at God's command and became an idol (2 Kings 18:4), and the calf was offered as a feast to the LORD. Religion itself, the nation, the family, a church tradition, a political cause, or a theological system can take the place of God while using his name. The prophets aimed their sharpest warnings at God's own people, not at outsiders, and the church has read them as warnings to itself. A last error is the pride that sees idols only in others' hearts. John's closing word, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21), is addressed to believers.
life:
The doctrine of idolatry gives a person a searching question: what do I trust to save me, what do I fear to lose, and what would I sacrifice almost anything to keep? Scripture's answer is that anything other than God that holds that place will eventually disappoint and diminish the one who serves it, because people become like what they worship. Money, approval, success, comfort, a relationship, or a cause can all become gods, not because they are bad but because they are asked to do what only God can do. Recognizing them is the first step, and the prophets' remedy is not only to smash the idol but to return to the fountain of living water. Idols are displaced by a greater love more than by willpower.

The doctrine also shapes worship and hope. Because God is known by his word and has shown his face in Jesus Christ, Christians worship not a God of their own design but the one who has made himself known. Because the Bible promises to cleanse God's people from their idols and give them a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25-26), the struggle against idolatry is carried on in hope, not despair. The story ends with people who once bowed to what could not see seeing the face of God, and being made like him.
questions: The golden calf was made while the people proclaimed a feast to the LORD. In what ways can people worship the true God on their own terms, through images or ideas of their own making?
Psalm 115 says that those who make idols become like them. What are some things people commonly trust or serve today, and how might they shape those who serve them?
Paul says both that an idol is nothing and that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons. How do those two statements help Christians think about customs and practices in their own culture?
